candidate_payload.early_body_text: l upus (2004) 13, 215 www.lupus-journal.com letter to the editor lupus revealing itself after a stiff-person syndrome sir—a 42-year old west indian man gradually developed, over a six month period, symmetrical muscles stiffness with painful spasms and intense asthenia leading to his hospitalization. physical examination found a lumbar hyperlordosis with rigidity of the lumbar, cervical, paraspinal and proximal leg muscles. blood cell count, as well as renal, hepatic and thyroid function and immunological investigations were normal. hiv and htlv1 serologies were negative. the presence of autoantibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase (gad) in both serum and cerebrospinal  uid led to the diagnosis of stiffperson syndrome (sps). no autoimmune or neoplastic disease was associated. a clinical improvement occurred in a few days with diazepam (40 mg/day at the beginning) and gabapentine. eighteen months later, the patient was again hospitalized for diffuse myalgias, abdominal pains, cutaneous rash, fever and weight loss of 16 kg. biological analyses showed an increase of in ammatory parameters (esr was 97 mm/1st h) and a pancytopenia with lymphopenia (890/mm3). all immunological  ndings including anti-nuclear antibodies (ana), antibodies directed against dsdna and extractable nuclear antigens (anti-ribonucleoprotein, anti-sjögren syndrome a and b, anti-smooth muscle and anti-scl-70) were positive. levels of c2, c3 and c4 components of complement were low. renal insuf ciency with proteinuria led to a biopsy that showed a class v who lupus glomerulonephritis. this systemic lupus erythematosus (sle) with severe renal involvement was initially treated by corticosteroids (1 mg/kg/ day) and antimalarial drug (hydroxychloroquine, 400 mg/day). due to a lack of ef ciency, treatment with 350 mg/m2 pulse cyclophosphamide monthly was started. clinical improvement was observed, and except anti-gad antibodies, all autoantibody populations mentioned previously became negative. the sps is a rare and disabling neurological disorder that generally occurs in young adults. this disease is characterized by progressive and involuntary muscle rigidity, accompanied by painful spasms. symptomatology is precipitated by stimuli (startling noises, emotion) and disappears during sleep. 1 in contrast to a tetanic attack, muscles of the face are not involved. the cause of the sps is unknown, but an autoimmune pathogenesis is suspected because of its frequent association (in about 60% of patients)2 with other autoimmune conditions such as type 1 diabetes3 or autoimmune thyroiditis, and the presence of antibodies recognizing gad, an enzyme involved in the synthesis of the inhibitory neurotransmitter gamma-aminobutyric acid (gaba). gaba reduction seems to play a major role in the manifestation of the stiffness by reducing the presynaptic inhibition on the motoneurons. presence of ana in the serum of a patient with sps has rarely been reported. 1 association of an sps with sle has never been described. we report herein the case of a patient who developed sle in the context of an explosive autoimmunity following in a few months with an sps. sle has probably not been induced by the treatment prescribed for sps because the drugs are not known to be responsible for drug-induced lupus, neither for an increase in ana titres. moreover, search for anti-histone antibodies was negative. thus, the presence of anti-gad antibodies during sps should trigger suspicion of an underlying sle, leading to a closer monitoring of the patient. references 1 levy lm, dalakas mc, floeter mk. the stiff-person syndrome: an autoimmune disorder affecting neurotransmission of gammaaminobutyric acid.
